blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design the core matching engine behind an online stock brokerage platform. Traders place buy and sell orders for a stock, and the system needs to match compatible orders against each other, the way a real exchange does, rather than simply recording a wish list. A limit order only trades at its specified price or better and waits patiently in the order book if nothing matches yet; a market order trades immediately at whatever price is currently available, sweeping through the book until it is filled or the book runs dry.

  • Actors: Trader (places orders), BrokerageService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: a price-time-priority order book per stock symbol, limit and market order matching, partial fills, and account cash and share tracking.

The distinguishing mechanic is a real matching engine: incoming orders sweep the opposite side of a live order book, execute trades at the resting order's price, and either rest the leftover quantity (limit orders) or cancel it (market orders), the same core algorithm every real stock exchange runs.
2. Functional Requirements
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Place a limit order: a trader specifies a symbol, side, quantity, and a price limit; it trades immediately against any acceptable resting orders and rests any leftover quantity in the book.
Place a market order: a trader specifies a symbol, side, and quantity; it trades immediately at whatever prices are currently available, with no price limit.

Match orders: a new order sweeps the opposite side of the book, executing one or more trades at the resting orders' prices, using price-time priority (best price first, earliest order first among equal prices).
Track holdings: every executed trade updates both parties' cash balance and share holdings accordingly.
Validate before accepting: a buy order is rejected if the account cannot afford it, and a sell order is rejected if the account does not hold enough shares.

blocks.text: 3. Non-Functional Requirements
Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many symbols, each with its own order book, must not require touching existing matching logic.
Extensibility: a new order type (stop orders, fill-or-kill) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: order-type execution rules, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: finding the best matching price on one side of the book is proportional to the number of resting orders on that side.
Thread safety: two orders on the same symbol submitted concurrently must resolve against a single, consistent view of that symbol's book.

blocks.text: 4. Clarifying Questions
Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Should the matching price be the resting order's price, the incoming order's price, or the midpoint, when the two differ?
Can a trader cancel or modify a resting order after placing it?
Should short selling (selling shares the account does not currently hold) be supported?
Is margin trading (buying with borrowed funds) in scope, or is every trade fully funded by cash on hand?
Should the system support additional order types like stop-loss or fill-or-kill?

blocks.text: 5. Assumptions & Constraints
To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: A matched trade always executes at the resting order's price, the standard price-time-priority convention, never the incoming order's price.
Order cancellation and modification are out of scope for this design, noted as a follow-up.
Short selling is not supported; a sell order is rejected outright if the account does not currently hold enough shares.
Every order is fully funded by cash on hand; margin trading is out of scope.
Only limit and market order types are modeled; stop orders and other conditional order types are noted as future extensions.

blocks.text: 6. Core Entities
The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Account, Order, OrderBook, and Trade

items: Account: a trader's cash balance and per-symbol share holdings.
Order: a buy or sell request for a symbol, with a type, an optional price, and remaining quantity.
OrderBook: one per symbol, holding every currently resting buy and sell order.
Trade: the result of matching a buy order against a sell order at a specific price and quantity.

blocks.text: 7. Relationships Between Entities
These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: An account places many orders; each order belongs to one symbol's order book; matches in that book produce trades referencing the two matched orders

items: Account to Order is one-to-many.
Order to OrderBook is many-to-one, scoped by symbol.
OrderBook to Trade is a production relationship: every match generates a trade referencing its buy and sell order.

blocks.text: 9. Design Patterns Used
Three patterns keep order-type execution rules, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.
9.1 Strategy Pattern (Order Execution Rules)

Why needed: a limit order and a market order fundamentally disagree on two questions: is this resting price acceptable to trade against, and should any unfilled leftover quantity wait in the book or simply cancel. Those two questions are exactly what varies by order type.

metadata.alt: OrderExecutionStrategy interface with LimitOrderExecutionStrategy and MarketOrderExecutionStrategy implementations

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new order type (stop-loss, fill-or-kill) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to the core matching loop in BrokerageService. What it solves: it isolates order-type-specific rules from the shared, stable sweep-and-match algorithm.
9.2 Observer Pattern (Notifications)
Why needed: an order being placed, rejected, or matched into a trade are all events a real trading platform would want to react to (portfolio updates, trade confirmations, price alerts).

metadata.alt: TradingObserver interface notified by BrokerageService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: BrokerageService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core matching workflow from side effects.
9.3 Factory Pattern (Id Creation)
Why needed: order and trade id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: OrderIdFactory generating sequential ORD and TRD prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every order and trade is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
10. Class Design
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Account: attributes accountId, cashBalance, holdings; responsibility: track one trader's buying power and share positions.
Order: attributes orderId, accountId, symbol, side, type, price, remainingQuantity, status; responsibility: represent one order through its entire matching lifecycle.
OrderBook: attributes symbol, buyOrders, sellOrders; responsibility: hold every resting order for one symbol.
Trade: attributes tradeId, buyOrderId, sellOrderId, price, quantity; responsibility: record one executed match.
BrokerageService: the orchestrator; responsibility: validate orders, run the sweep-and-match algorithm, update accounts, and notify observers.

blocks.text: 11. Interface Design
Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: OrderExecutionStrategy and TradingObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: OrderExecutionStrategy: priceAcceptable(order, restingPrice) and restsInBookIfUnfilled(): abstract away exactly what makes a resting price tradeable for this order type, and what happens to any leftover quantity.
TradingObserver: onOrderPlaced / onOrderRejected / onTradeExecuted: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: 13. Important Workflows
The sweep-and-match workflow, alongside its rejection branches, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Validate affordability, sweep the opposite book side for acceptable matches, execute trades, then rest or cancel any leftover quantity depending on order type

items: Happy path with a match: place order → affordable → a resting order at an acceptable price is found → execute a trade at the resting price → repeat until filled or no more acceptable matches.
Happy path with no match: place order → affordable → no acceptable resting order found → for a limit order, rest the full quantity in the book; for a market order, cancel the unfilled quantity.
Rejection paths: place order → cannot afford it (buy) or does not hold enough shares (sell) → rejected before any matching is attempted.

blocks.text: 14. Public APIs / Methods
The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: placeOrder(accountId, symbol, side, type, price, quantity): validates, matches, and either rests or resolves the order, returning its final state.

blocks.text: 15. Exception Handling
Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: InsufficientFundsException: a buy order's cost would exceed the account's available cash.
InsufficientSharesException: a sell order's quantity exceeds the account's currently held shares.
InvalidOrderException: an unknown order id.

blocks.text: 16. Concurrency Considerations
The critical race is two orders on the same symbol submitted at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to place an order on the same symbol; synchronization ensures one order matches against a consistent book state before the other is processed

blocks.text: Synchronizing the sweep-and-match step per symbol ensures the order book is never read and updated inconsistently, so two concurrent orders can never both match against the exact same resting quantity.
17. Extensibility Discussion
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new order type (stop-loss, fill-or-kill, all-or-none) is a new OrderExecutionStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (trade confirmation email, price alert) is a new TradingObserver implementation.
Order cancellation can be added as a new service method that simply removes a resting order from its book without touching the matching algorithm.
Short selling can be layered on by relaxing the share-sufficiency check for accounts opted into margin trading.

blocks.text: 18. SOLID Principles Applied

items: Single Responsibility: OrderBook tracks resting orders, OrderExecutionStrategy decides order-type rules, TradingObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new order types or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to BrokerageService.
Liskov Substitution: any OrderExecutionStrategy or TradingObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: TradingObserver exposes only the three lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: BrokerageService depends on the OrderExecutionStrategy and TradingObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.

blocks.text: 19. Edge Cases

items: A market order placed against an empty opposite book simply fills zero shares and cancels entirely, since a market order never rests.
A limit order whose price exactly equals a resting order's price is a valid match, using an inclusive price comparison.
A single incoming order matches against multiple resting orders in sequence until fully filled, generating multiple trades from one placeOrder call.
An account placing a buy order for a stock it already holds shares of is treated identically to any other buy order, cash affordability is the only gate.

blocks.text: 20. Complexity Analysis

items: placeOrder: O(k) where k is the number of resting orders matched against, bounded by the total resting orders on the opposite side in the worst case.
Space: O(accounts + resting orders + trades) held in memory.

blocks.text: 21. Database Design
A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Account, Order, Trade, and a Holding table for per symbol share counts

items: An index on Order(symbol, side, status) speeds up scanning the correct side of a symbol's book for matches.
Holding is a separate table keyed by (accountId, symbol), since an account can hold many different symbols.

blocks.text: 22. Improvements & Follow-Up Questions

items: Support order cancellation and modification for resting orders.
Add stop-loss and fill-or-kill order types as additional OrderExecutionStrategy implementations.
Support short selling and margin trading with proper risk controls.
In a distributed deployment, shard order books by symbol across multiple matching engine instances rather than a single in-process lock per symbol.

from enum import Enum

# Which direction an order trades.
class OrderSide(Enum):
    BUY = "BUY"
    SELL = "SELL"

# Whether an order has a price limit or trades at any available price.
class OrderType(Enum):
    LIMIT = "LIMIT"
    MARKET = "MARKET"

# Lifecycle status of a single order.
class OrderStatus(Enum):
    OPEN = "OPEN"                          # resting in the book, no fills yet
    PARTIALLY_FILLED = "PARTIALLY_FILLED"  # some quantity matched, some still resting
    FILLED = "FILLED"                      # fully matched
    CANCELLED = "CANCELLED"                # unfilled remainder cancelled, e.g. an unfilled market order

# A trader's cash balance and per symbol share holdings.
class Account:
    def __init__(self, account_id, cash_balance):
        self.account_id = account_id      # unique id
        self.cash_balance = cash_balance    # available cash
        self.holdings = {}                    # symbol -> shares held

    def adjust_cash(self, amount):
        self.cash_balance += amount  # add or subtract cash

    def get_shares(self, symbol):
        return self.holdings.get(symbol, 0)  # shares getter

    def adjust_shares(self, symbol, amount):
        self.holdings[symbol] = self.holdings.get(symbol, 0) + amount  # add or subtract shares

# A single buy or sell order for one symbol.
class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id, account_id, symbol, side, order_type, price, quantity):
        self.order_id = order_id          # unique id, e.g. ORD1
        self.account_id = account_id        # who placed it
        self.symbol = symbol                  # which stock
        self.side = side                        # buy or sell
        self.type = order_type                    # limit or market
        self.price = price                          # limit price, ignored for market orders
        self.remaining_quantity = quantity            # starts fully unfilled
        self.status = OrderStatus.OPEN                  # starts open

    def reduce_quantity(self, amount):
        self.remaining_quantity -= amount  # apply a fill

# The result of matching a buy order against a sell order.
class Trade:
    def __init__(self, trade_id, buy_order_id, sell_order_id, price, quantity):
        self.trade_id = trade_id          # unique id, e.g. TRD1
        self.buy_order_id = buy_order_id    # the matched buy order
        self.sell_order_id = sell_order_id    # the matched sell order
        self.price = price                      # execution price, the resting order's price
        self.quantity = quantity                  # shares exchanged in this trade

# Creates sequential, correctly-prefixed ids for orders and trades.
class OrderIdFactory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.order_counter = 0  # running id counter for orders
        self.trade_counter = 0    # running id counter for trades

    def next_order_id(self):
        self.order_counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return f"ORD{self.order_counter}"  # e.g. ORD1

    def next_trade_id(self):
        self.trade_counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return f"TRD{self.trade_counter}"  # e.g. TRD1

codes.python:
# Holds every currently resting buy and sell order for one symbol.
class OrderBook:
    def __init__(self, symbol):
        self.symbol = symbol      # which stock this book is for
        self.buy_orders = []        # resting buy orders
        self.sell_orders = []         # resting sell orders

    def best_ask(self):
        best = None                                                # best sell order found so far
        for o in self.sell_orders:                                    # scan every resting sell order
            if o.remaining_quantity <= 0:
                continue  # skip fully filled ones
            if best is None or o.price < best.price:
                best = o  # lower price wins
        return best  # the cheapest resting sell order, or None if none remain

    def best_bid(self):
        best = None                                                # best buy order found so far
        for o in self.buy_orders:                                     # scan every resting buy order
            if o.remaining_quantity <= 0:
                continue  # skip fully filled ones
            if best is None or o.price > best.price:
                best = o  # higher price wins
        return best  # the most generous resting buy order, or None if none remain

# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class InsufficientFundsException(Exception): pass
class InsufficientSharesException(Exception): pass
class InvalidOrderException(Exception): pass

# The core matching engine tying every piece together.
class BrokerageService:
    def __init__(self):
        self.accounts = {}        # accountId -> Account
        self.order_books = {}       # symbol -> OrderBook
        self.observers = []           # listeners

    def add_account(self, account):
        self.accounts[account.account_id] = account  # register an account

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def _book_for(self, symbol):
        if symbol not in self.order_books:
            self.order_books[symbol] = OrderBook(symbol)  # create the book on first use
        return self.order_books[symbol]

    def _strategy_for(self, order_type):
        return LimitOrderExecutionStrategy() if order_type == OrderType.LIMIT else MarketOrderExecutionStrategy()

    def place_order(self, account_id, symbol, side, order_type, price, quantity, factory):
        account = self.accounts[account_id]  # look up account
        if side == OrderSide.BUY:  # buying needs enough cash
            estimated_cost = price * quantity  # worst case cost estimate
            if account.cash_balance < estimated_cost:  # not enough cash
                for obs in self.observers:
                    obs.on_order_rejected(account_id, "Insufficient funds")  # notify
                raise InsufficientFundsException(f"Not enough cash for {account_id}")
        else:  # selling needs enough shares
            if account.get_shares(symbol) < quantity:  # not enough shares
                for obs in self.observers:
                    obs.on_order_rejected(account_id, "Insufficient shares")  # notify
                raise InsufficientSharesException(f"Not enough shares for {account_id}")
        order_id = factory.next_order_id()  # build id
        order = Order(order_id, account_id, symbol, side, order_type, price, quantity)  # build order
        book = self._book_for(symbol)  # this symbol's book
        strategy = self._strategy_for(order_type)  # order-type rules
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_order_placed(order)  # notify

        while order.remaining_quantity > 0:  # keep sweeping while unfilled
            resting_match = book.best_ask() if side == OrderSide.BUY else book.best_bid()  # best available opposite order
            if resting_match is None or not strategy.price_acceptable(order, resting_match.price):
                break  # nothing left to match
            fill_quantity = min(order.remaining_quantity, resting_match.remaining_quantity)  # how much trades now
            execution_price = resting_match.price  # always the resting order's price
            order.reduce_quantity(fill_quantity)  # apply the fill to the incoming order
            resting_match.reduce_quantity(fill_quantity)  # apply the fill to the resting order
            resting_match.status = OrderStatus.FILLED if resting_match.remaining_quantity == 0 else OrderStatus.PARTIALLY_FILLED  # update resting order's status
            buy_order_id = order.order_id if side == OrderSide.BUY else resting_match.order_id  # which side is the buyer
            sell_order_id = resting_match.order_id if side == OrderSide.BUY else order.order_id  # which side is the seller
            trade = Trade(factory.next_trade_id(), buy_order_id, sell_order_id, execution_price, fill_quantity)  # record the trade
            buyer_account = self.accounts[account_id if side == OrderSide.BUY else resting_match.account_id]  # the buying account
            seller_account = self.accounts[resting_match.account_id if side == OrderSide.BUY else account_id]  # the selling account
            buyer_account.adjust_cash(-execution_price * fill_quantity)  # buyer pays cash
            buyer_account.adjust_shares(symbol, fill_quantity)  # buyer receives shares
            seller_account.adjust_cash(execution_price * fill_quantity)  # seller receives cash
            seller_account.adjust_shares(symbol, -fill_quantity)  # seller gives up shares
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_trade_executed(trade)  # notify

        if order.remaining_quantity > 0:  # still unfilled after sweeping
            if strategy.rests_in_book_if_unfilled():  # this order type rests
                order.status = OrderStatus.OPEN if order.remaining_quantity == quantity else OrderStatus.PARTIALLY_FILLED  # open or partially filled
                (book.buy_orders if side == OrderSide.BUY else book.sell_orders).append(order)  # add to this order's own side
            else:  # this order type cancels
                order.status = OrderStatus.CANCELLED  # unfilled remainder cancels
        else:  # fully filled
            order.status = OrderStatus.FILLED
        return order  # hand back the final order state

blocks.text: Interview Discussion Points

items: Why does a trade always execute at the resting order's price rather than the incoming order's price? Because the resting order was there first and already published its acceptable price to the market; the incoming order is the one choosing to trade against it, so it gets the better (or equal) deal, the standard convention on every real exchange.

Why does a market order never rest in the book? Because a market order's entire purpose is immediate execution at whatever price is available right now; letting it wait would contradict what a trader is actually asking for, which is why it cancels its unfilled remainder instead.

How would you extend this to support order cancellation? Add a cancelOrder method that removes a resting order from its book's list by id, with no interaction with the matching algorithm itself since a cancelled order is simply no longer scanned.

blocks.text: Trade-offs & Alternative Designs

items: O(n) linear scan for the best price vs a sorted data structure (heap or balanced tree): a linear scan is simple to implement correctly and reason about at small to moderate order book depth, at the cost of scaling worse than a proper price-indexed structure would at real-exchange volumes.

Resting-order-price execution vs midpoint pricing: resting-order pricing is simple and matches real exchange convention, giving a clear, deterministic answer for every trade; midpoint pricing could arguably be "fairer" to both sides but is not how real order-driven markets actually work.

No short selling vs supporting it: disallowing short selling keeps the share-sufficiency check simple and prevents an account from having negative holdings, at the cost of not supporting a real and common trading strategy that a production brokerage would need.

blocks.text: Production Considerations & Best Practices

items: Persist accounts, orders, and trades in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.

Emit order/trade events to a message queue so downstream systems (trade confirmations, portfolio recalculation, regulatory reporting) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to placeOrder so retried network requests cannot double-submit the same order.
Expose metrics on order book depth and match latency per symbol, which reveal which symbols need dedicated matching engine capacity.
